title: Python coding interview practice
summary: Practise solving coding problems out loud — clarify, plan, code clean Python, test edge cases, and talk through trade-offs like an engineer.
objectives: Follow a repeatable problem-solving framework under interview pressure
Clarify the problem and state assumptions before writing code
Reason about time and space complexity using Big-O notation
Pick the right built-in data structure: list, dict, set, deque
Write clean, readable Python and test edge cases out loud
Recover gracefully when you get stuck or hit a bug

quiz.q: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a Python dict?
quiz.why: Dicts are hash maps, so average key lookup is constant time O(1) — a core reason to reach for them in interviews.

quiz.q: Which data structure gives O(1) membership tests and removes duplicates?
quiz.why: A set stores unique hashable items and supports O(1) average 'in' checks, unlike a list which is O(n).

quiz.q: Before writing any code in an interview, what should you do first?
options: Clarify the problem and ask about inputs and edge cases
Stay silent until you have the full answer
quiz.why: Clarifying inputs, output, constraints and edge cases shows engineering judgement and prevents solving the wrong problem.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is Big-O notation used for?
quiz.answer: It describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input size grows.
quiz.why: Big-O focuses on growth rate for large inputs, ignoring constants, so you can compare approaches.

quiz.q: Name one edge case worth checking on a function that processes a list of numbers.
quiz.answer: An empty list (also valid: a single element, negatives, duplicates, or very large input).
quiz.why: Empty and single-element inputs are the classic cases that break naive code and impress interviewers when handled.

quiz.q: If you get stuck mid-problem, what is the best move?
options: Talk through your thinking and state a simpler brute-force first
Ask the interviewer for the answer
quiz.why: Interviewers score your communication and process; a working brute-force you can explain beats silent perfection you never reach.

body_markdown:
## What a coding interview really tests

A coding interview is **not** a test of whether you've memorised the answer. It tests how you *think*: can you understand a problem, break it down, write clean code, and communicate while you do it? As a maths graduate you already have the strongest muscle — structured problem solving. Now you add a spoken process and fluent Python.

The single biggest mistake beginners make is going silent and typing. Interviewers can't read your mind. **Narrate everything.**

## A framework you can repeat

Use the same five steps on every problem so nerves don't derail you:

1. **Clarify** — restate the problem, ask about input types, size, and edge cases.
2. **Examples** — work a small example by hand to confirm understanding.
3. **Plan** — describe an approach in plain English before coding; mention the Big-O.
4. **Code** — write clean Python, talking as you go.
5. **Test** — run through edge cases out loud: empty input, one element, duplicates.

It is completely fine to start with a brute-force solution, say so, then improve it.

## Big-O in one minute

**Big-O** describes how running time grows as input size *n* grows. You compare approaches by their growth, ignoring constants.

- `O(1)` — constant, e.g. a dict lookup.
- `O(n)` — one pass through the data.
- `O(n log n)` — typical sorting.
- `O(n^2)` — nested loops over the same data; usually a red flag you can improve.

## Know your data structures

Most interview wins come from picking the right built-in. A **dict** or **set** turns an O(n^2) scan into an O(n) pass.

```python
# Two-sum: find indices of two numbers adding to target.
def two_sum(nums, target):
    seen = {}                      # value -> index
    for i, x in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - x
        if need in seen:           # O(1) lookup
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[x] = i
    return []                      # no pair found

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))  # [0, 1]
```

The naive version checks every pair in O(n^2); the dict version is a single O(n) pass.

## Test edge cases out loud

After coding, walk through inputs that break naive code. State each one and check your code handles it.

```python
assert two_sum([], 5) == []          # empty list
assert two_sum([3], 3) == []         # single element
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1]  # duplicates
print("all checks pass")
```

## Practise deliberately

Don't grind hundreds of random problems. Pick a pattern — hash maps, two pointers, sliding window, binary search — and do three or four problems on it until it feels automatic. Solve them *out loud*, even alone, and time yourself. The goal is fluency under pressure, not coverage.

slides.title: Narrate everything
bullets: Process matters as much as the answer.
slides.narration: Here is the single biggest mistake beginners make: they go quiet and start typing. The interviewer cannot read your mind, so a silent perfect answer scores worse than an out-loud decent one. Narrate every assumption and every decision. Your process is being graded as much as your code.

Plan in plain English, mention Big-O.

slides.title: Big-O in one minute
bullets: Describes growth as input n grows.
O(n log n) sorting, O(n^2) nested loops.
slides.narration: Big-O describes how running time grows as the input grows. Constant time is order one, a single pass is order n, typical sorting is n log n, and nested loops over the same data are order n squared. That last one is usually a sign you can do better. You ignore constants and compare the growth.

slides.title: Pick the right structure
bullets: deque: fast appends and pops at both ends.
slides.narration: Most interview wins come from choosing the right built-in. A dictionary gives constant-time lookups. A set gives constant-time membership tests and removes duplicates. A list is ordered but checking membership is a slow linear scan. And a deque, spelled d-e-q-u-e, is great for fast operations at both ends.

slides.title: Hash map example
bullets: Two-sum: find a pair summing to target.
A dict makes it a single O(n) pass.
slides.narration: Here's the classic two-sum. We want two numbers that add to a target. The naive way checks every pair, which is order n squared. Instead we keep a dictionary of values we've already seen. For each number we ask: have I already seen its complement? That lookup is constant time, so the whole thing is a single order n pass.

slides.title: Test edge cases out loud
bullets: State each case as you check it.
slides.code:
assert two_sum([], 5) == []
assert two_sum([3], 3) == []
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1]
print("all checks pass")
slides.narration: After you code, walk through the inputs that break naive solutions, and say each one aloud. What about an empty list? A single element? Duplicates? Negative numbers? A quick set of asserts proves your function holds up, and narrating them shows the interviewer you think like an engineer.

slides.title: When you get stuck
bullets: Don't go silent or wipe everything.
A working slow answer beats none.
slides.narration: Everyone gets stuck. The wrong move is to go quiet or erase everything and restart. Instead, say out loud where you're stuck, and offer a simpler brute-force you can actually finish. A working slow answer you can explain beats a perfect one you never reach. Interviewers often nudge you if you're clearly thinking.

slides.title: Practise deliberately
bullets: Master one pattern at a time.
Solve out loud and time yourself.
slides.narration: Finally, practise with intent. Don't grind hundreds of random problems. Pick one pattern, like hash maps or two pointers, and do three or four until it feels automatic. Solve them out loud even when alone, and time yourself. The goal is fluency under pressure, not raw coverage.
